lead: A Bode plot draws the open-loop frequency response G(jω) as two graphs: gain in decibels and phase in degrees, both against a logarithmic frequency axis. It exists to turn multiplication of complex factors into addition of straight-line segments. Engineers use it to sketch a transfer function by hand, to see which corner frequencies dominate, and to read closed-loop stability from the 0 dB and −180° crossings. The same curves guide loop shaping in motor drives, power supplies and process loops.
prereq: You need: 4.1 Frequency response, the transfer function from Unit 1, and basic logarithms and decibels.

sections.h3: Gain in decibels and the log frequency axis

blocks.text: A Bode plot shows open-loop G(jω) as two curves: magnitude and phase, both against frequency on a log axis. Magnitude is in decibels: |G|<sub>dB</sub> = 20 log<sub>10</sub> |G(jω)|. Phase is ∠G(jω) in degrees. The frequency axis uses log<sub>10</sub>(ω). Equal distances mean equal ratios; one decade is ×10 in frequency. This matters because a simple pole (1+jωT)<sup>−1</sup> changes gain by −20 dB/decade after ω=1/T. Multiplication of magnitudes becomes addition of dB values: 20 log<sub>10</sub>|G<sub>1</sub>G<sub>2</sub>| = 20 log<sub>10</sub>|G<sub>1</sub>| + 20 log<sub>10</sub>|G<sub>2</sub>|. On a log frequency axis the straight-line asymptotes of each factor add. One pole at the origin gives −20 dB/decade and −90°; one zero at the origin gives +20 dB/decade and +90°. Use this for hand sketches and for reading loop gain on a servo or power-supply loop.

Each factor in G(jω) has a low-frequency asymptote and a corner. Here T is a time constant in seconds, ω<sub>n</sub> is a natural frequency in rad/s, ζ is dimensionless damping ratio, and K is the constant gain.

At a simple-pole corner the exact gain is −3 dB, not 0 dB; the asymptote is a sketch. A quadratic pole can peak near ω<sub>n</sub> when ζ is small; the asymptotic slope still changes by −40 dB/decade. Constant K moves the whole magnitude curve up or down without changing any slope.

items: Write G(s) in time-constant form, with factors (1+sT) and quadratic factors.
Find the low-frequency gain: put s→0. If there are n poles at the origin, start with slope −20n dB/decade; m zeros at the origin give +20m.
Mark every corner: 1/T for a simple factor, ω<sub>n</sub> for a quadratic factor.
Draw the asymptote from left to right. At each corner add slope: +20 for a simple zero, −20 for a simple pole, +40 for a quadratic zero, −40 for a quadratic pole.
Draw phase by adding each factor’s phase; the phase curve is smooth, not a step.

Read stability for an open-loop stable system: find gain crossover ωgc where |G|dB=0 and phase crossover ωpc where ∠G=−180°. Closed-loop stability needs the 0 dB crossing to occur before phase reaches −180°, or gain below 0 dB at ωpc. Margins are quantified in 4.6.

blocks.text: From asymptotes to transfer function: the low-frequency line gives K/sn; each slope change gives a factor. A −20 dB/decade change at ωc is a simple pole with T=1/ωc; +20 is a simple zero; ±40 is a quadratic pair. Some syllabi call this the Bode plot approach. Polar plots in 4.4 and Nyquist plots in 4.5 show the same data in one complex-plane curve.

figure.caption: The straight-line asymptotes for G(s)=100/((s+1)(s+10)): flat at 20 dB up to 1 rad/s, then −20 dB/decade, then −40 dB/decade after 10 rad/s.

spec.aria: Straight-line Bode magnitude asymptotes: flat at 20 dB, then falling 20 dB per decade after 1 rad/s and 40 dB per decade after 10 rad/s.

examples.question: The open-loop transfer function of a unity-feedback system is G(s)=100/((s+1)(s+10)). (a) Sketch its asymptotic Bode magnitude plot, marking low-frequency gain, corner frequencies and slopes. (b) Find the exact gain crossover frequency and the phase there.
steps: Low-frequency gain: put s=0. G(0)=10. In dB: 20 log<sub>10</sub>(10)=20 dB.
Corners: first factor (1+s) has corner ω=1 rad/s. Second factor (1+s/10) has T<sub>2</sub>=0.1 s, so corner ω=1/T<sub>2</sub>=10 rad/s.

Slopes: below 1 rad/s, 0 dB/decade. Between 1 and 10 rad/s, one simple pole adds −20 dB/decade, so slope is −20 dB/decade. Above 10 rad/s, the second simple pole adds another −20 dB/decade, so slope is −40 dB/decade. The asymptote passes 20 dB at ω=1, 0 dB at ω=10, and −40 dB at ω=100 rad/s.
examples.answer: Low-frequency gain 20 dB; corners at 1 and 10 rad/s (T<sub>2</sub>=0.1 s); slopes 0, −20 and −40 dB/decade; exact gain crossover ω<sub>gc</sub>=7.82 rad/s; phase there −120.7°.
examples.check:
import math
low = 20*math.log10(10)
w1 = 1.0
T2 = 0.1
slope1 = -20.0
slope2 = -40.0
x = (-101 + math.sqrt(101**2 + 4*9900))/2
wgc = math.sqrt(x)
phase = -(math.degrees(math.atan(wgc)) + math.degrees(math.atan(wgc/10)))
print(f'{low:.1f}')
print(f'{w1:.1f}')
print(f'{T2:.1f}')
print(f'{slope1:.1f}')
print(f'{slope2:.1f}')
print(f'{wgc:.2f}')
print(f'{phase:.1f}')

traps: Magnitude in dB uses 20 log<sub>10</sub>, not 10 log<sub>10</sub>. The 10 log<sub>10</sub> form is for power.
The corner of (1+jωT) is at ω=1/T, not at T. Slopes are per decade, not per octave; −20 dB/decade is about −6 dB/octave.
An asymptotic 0 dB crossing is only an estimate. A nearby corner lowers or raises the exact curve, so the exact gain crossover can move; solve |G(jω)|=1 when asked.
The initial slope comes from poles or zeros at the origin: n poles give −20n dB/decade, m zeros give +20m dB/decade. Constant K shifts the curve vertically and does not change slope.
At a simple-pole corner the phase is −45°, not −90°. The phase reaches −90° only as ω becomes much larger than the corner.

quiz.q: What is the dB formula for magnitude |G(jω)|?
quiz.a: 20 log<sub>10</sub> |G(jω)|. The 10 log<sub>10</sub> form is for power.

quiz.q: What is the phase contribution of a pole at the origin?
quiz.a: −90° at all frequencies; a zero at the origin gives +90°.

quiz.q: Why is the frequency axis logarithmic?
quiz.a: Equal distances become equal frequency ratios; a decade is ×10. Each simple pole or zero then gives a constant slope of ±20 dB/decade, so asymptotes add as straight lines.

quiz.q: For G(s)=50/((s+2)(s+20)), find the low-frequency gain in dB and the corner frequencies.
quiz.a: Low-frequency gain =50/(2×20)=1.25; 20 log<sub>10</sub>(1.25)=1.94 dB. Corners at 2 and 20 rad/s. Slopes are 0, −20 and −40 dB/decade.

quiz.q: A simple pole factor has corner at 10 rad/s. State its slope after the corner, its phase at the corner, and its exact gain at the corner.
quiz.a: Slope after corner: −20 dB/decade. Phase at corner: −45°. Exact gain at corner: −3 dB relative to the low-frequency asymptote.

quiz.q: A Bode magnitude starts at −20 dB/decade, changes to −40 dB/decade at 2 rad/s, then to −20 dB/decade at 20 rad/s. Identify the factors.
quiz.a: One pole at the origin, one simple pole at 2 rad/s, and one simple zero at 20 rad/s. Form: K(1+s/20)/(s(1+s/2)).

quiz.q: At phase crossover, ∠G=−180° and |G|<sub>dB</sub>=−5 dB. Is the closed-loop system stable if the open-loop plant is stable?
quiz.a: Yes for that gain. The gain at the critical phase is below 0 dB, so the critical point is not enclosed. The gain margin is +5 dB; margin formulas are in 4.6.

beyond: Not for the exam. Bode plots remain the standard interface in loop-shaping tools: MATLAB's bode and Python's control.bode plot the same asymptotes you sketch by hand. Power-electronics engineers use the gain and phase curves to check converter stability over load and line changes. System-identification engineers fit a transfer function to measured frequency-response data from a sweep or a relay test. Search next for loop shaping, frequency response identification and the Bode sensitivity integral if you want the research side.
